endorsements.quote: Actions with potential clinical, regulatory, or operational impact—including staffing modifications, inventory procurement, workflow changes, or quality interventions—require explicit human approval before execution.

Every data request is authenticated using role-based access control (RBAC) and least-privilege permissions, ensuring that agents access only the minimum information necessary for their assigned functions.
Such recommendations can be evaluated retrospectively, tested in shadow mode, and progressively integrated into operations while maintaining human oversight.

Effective deployment therefore requires deliberate trust calibration, supported by transparent evidence and provenance, appropriately calibrated confidence estimates, tiered alerts, and monitoring of recommendation acceptance and override patterns.

Meaningful human oversight also requires adequate time and competency: laboratory personnel responsible for reviewing agent-generated findings should receive role-specific training, understand system limitations and escalation procedures, and have sufficient time to evaluate consequential recommendations rather than functioning as nominal approvers.

Effective collaboration therefore depends on transparent recommendations, calibrated confidence estimates, meaningful human oversight, and sufficient authority for laboratorians to accept, modify, or reject AI-generated recommendations.
Individual agents should be independently versioned, validated, monitored, and replaceable throughout their lifecycle.

Evaluation should also consider operational performance (e.g., TAT, workflow efficiency, and resource utilization), safety and quality (e.g., false alerts, missed events, and quality-management indicators), human factors (e.g., automation bias, alert fatigue, trust calibration, recommendation acceptance and override rates, time required for oversight, and user competency), and governance (e.g., audit completeness, provenance, and compliance).

Performance degradation or unexpected behavior should trigger predefined rollback or fallback mechanisms that preserve safe laboratory operation while allowing individual agents to evolve without disrupting the broader system.
The appropriate regulatory pathway will depend on the system’s intended use, degree of autonomy, and potential impact on patient care.

unlisted_practices: Evaluate agentic AI beyond prediction-performance metrics such as sensitivity and specificity.
Align agentic AI deployment with existing laboratory quality-management frameworks, including validation, risk management, nonconformity management, and continuous quality improvement.
Document structured provenance for every AI alert, including data sources, supporting evidence, confidence estimates, decision rules, and escalation triggers.
Validate agentic systems through staged pathway from retrospective validation to shadow deployment to recommendation-only use and limited automation, with prespecified acceptance criteria.
Execute AI-generated queries through a constrained, read-only access layer validated against approved schemas and block or escalate out-of-policy queries for human review.
Limit automated actions to predefined low-risk, reversible actions that are logged, auditable, and reversible.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual framework/perspective paper proposing an agentic framework (LabARIA) with transparent governance and human oversight for clinical laboratory medicine, rather than an empirical study or systematic review.
